## Stable isotope measurements

Sample preparation and analyse protocoles were previously published (@lauzent_etude_2017) and hereafter synthetised. 

Ground biological samples were defatted by accelerated solvent extraction (ASE; 100 °C, 100 bar) using dichloromethane prior to isotope analysis to minimize bias in δ¹³C measurements associated with the lower δ¹³C signature of lipids relative to other biochemical components. Sediments can contain highly variable amounts of carbonates, which can skew the δ¹³C value. For this reason, inorganic carbon was removed prior to δ¹³C analysis by adding 2 N HCl drop by drop until the effervescence ceased, followed by drying. The δ¹⁵N analyses were performed without this preliminary extraction. The material was then recovered, stored in microtubes and sample mass was adjusted when necessary according to matrix characteristics : approximately 15-20 mg for δ¹⁵N sediment analyses, 2 mg for for δ¹³C sediment analyses, and 0,2 mg ± 0,1 mg for δ¹⁵N and δ¹³C biota analyses.

Carbon and nitrogen stable isotope ratios were measured using a Thermo Finnigan Delta V Plus EA–IRMS coupled to a Conflo IV interface. Samples were flash-combusted at 1020 °C, with subsequent reduction at 650 °C and chromatographic separation of the resulting gases before IRMS analysis. Isotope-ratio calibration was performed using USG24 graphite for δ¹³C and IAEA-N2 ammonium sulfate for δ¹⁵N. Quality-control materials were analyzed every ten biological samples and every five sediment samples. Analytical precision, estimated from repeated analyses of reference materials, ranged from 0.19 to 0.34‰ for δ¹³C and from 0.23 to 0.29‰ for δ¹⁵N in the present study (@gallienEtudeComparativeLecodynamique2021).

## Lipid content measurements

Lipid content of fish and invertebrate samples was measured using a previously published procedure (@lauzent_etude_2017) hereafter synthetised. Lipid content was determined gravimetrically following accelerated solvent extraction (ASE). Approximately 0.1 g of dry sample was extracted with dichloromethane using a Dionex ASE 350 at 100 °C and 100 bar. Extracts were evaporated to dryness under nitrogen and the residue was weighed to constant mass. Lipid content was expressed as the percentage of extracted residue relative to sample dry mass.

## Chemical analysis

PCBs, PFASs and HBCDD isomers were extracted from sediment, benthic invertebrate, and fish samples and analysed following different previously published procedures for PFASs (@munozEcodynamiqueComposesPoly2015; @munozEvidenceTrophicTransfer2017; @gallienEtudeComparativeLecodynamique2021), PCBs (@lauzent_etude_2017), and HBCDD isomers(@lauzent_etude_2017), hereafter synthetised. 


### Extraction

To determine PFAS, PCB and HBCDD concentrations in the different matrices, contaminants were extracted using microwave-assisted solvent extraction. For all compound classes, homogenized samples were fortified with internal standards before extraction, followed by filtration through glass wool and concentration under nitrogen. Compound-specific solvents and cleanup procedures were then applied.

For PFAS, freeze-dried and homogenized samples (approximately 0.25 g for biota and 2 g for sediment) were extracted with methanol (13 mL for biota; 10 mL for sediment) at 70 °C, with a 5-min holding step followed by 10 min of cooling. For biota, extracts were diluted with 50 mL ultrapure water and purified using weak anion-exchange solid-phase extraction (Strata X-AW, Phenomenex) followed by graphitized carbon cleanup (ENVI-Carb, 250 mg/3 mL, Sigma-Aldrich). Analytes were eluted with two successive 4-mL volumes of methanol containing 0.2% ammonium hydroxide. Purified extracts were concentrated under nitrogen and transferred to polypropylene injection vials.

For PCBs and HBCDD isomers, freeze-dried and homogenized samples (approximately 0.5 g for biota and 1.5 g for sediment) were extracted with 12 mL dichloromethane at 80 °C, with a 5-min holding step followed by 5 min of cooling. Extracts were purified on microcolumns containing activated copper to remove sulfur and 40% H₂SO₄-acidified silica to remove lipids and other interfering compounds. Columns were conditioned with pentane, and analytes were eluted with three 5-mL portions of pentane/dichloromethane (90:10, v/v). The eluates were concentrated under nitrogen. For PCB analysis, extracts were reconstituted in 50–100 µL isooctane and spiked with an OCN syringe standard to assess extraction recovery, whereas HBCDD extracts were reconstituted in 50–100 µL methanol.

### Quantification

#### PFAS quantification

PFAS in sediment and biological samples were analysed by liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry(LC–ESI–MS/MS), using an Agilent 1200 LC system coupled to an Agilent 6490 triple-quadrupole mass spectrometer equipped with an Agilent Jet Stream electrospray ionization source. Chromatographic separation was performed on a Zorbax Eclipse Plus C18 analytical column, with a Poroshell 120 SB C18 guard column. The mobile phases consisted of Milli-Q water containing 2 mM ammonium acetate (A) and acetonitrile/water (95:5, v/v) containing 2 mM ammonium acetate (B). The ESI source was operated in negative-ion mode, and compounds were monitored using dynamic multiple reaction monitoring (MRM). A short C18 delay column was installed upstream of the analytical system to minimize background PFAS contamination. Isotopically labelled internal standards were used for quantification and to account for analytical variability.

#### PCB quantification

After the extraction step, PCB concentrations were determined by gas chromatography coupled with electron capture detection (GC–ECD) using an Agilent 6890N system. Extracts were injected in pulsed splitless mode onto a J&W HP-5MS capillary column (60 m × 0.25 mm × 0.1 µm; 5% phenyl–95% methylpolysiloxane). Helium was used as the carrier gas at 1.3 mL min⁻¹ and nitrogen as the make-up gas at 60 mL min⁻¹. Injector and detector temperatures were set at 280 and 300 °C, respectively. The oven temperature programme was: 90 °C for 2 min, ramped at 15 °C min⁻¹ to 178 °C, then at 2 °C min⁻¹ to 230 °C, and finally at 30 °C min⁻¹ to 300 °C, held for 3.8 min. The injection volume was 1 µL.


#### HBCDD quantification

The HBCDD analytical programme distinguished the three principal diastereoisomers, α-, β- and γ-HBCDD, allowing isomer-specific concentration profiles to be characterized.
After the extraction step, HBCDD isomers were analyzed by ultra-performance liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (UPLC–MS/MS), using an Acquity UPLC system coupled to a Quattro Premier XE triple-quadrupole mass spectrometer (Waters). Analytes were separated on a reversed-phase C18 column (Acquity UPLC BEH C18, 1.7 µm, 100 × 2.1 mm) using a methanol/water (70:30, v/v) and acetonitrile gradient at a flow rate of 0.3 mL min⁻¹. The injection volume was 5 µL, and analyses were performed in negative electrospray ionization mode. HBCDD isomers were monitored using the same quantification (m/z 640.5 → 81.0) and confirmation (m/z 640.5 → 79.0) transitions and were therefore distinguished based on chromatographic retention times.

### Analytical quality assurance and quality control

Analytical quality assurance included isotopically labelled internal standards added prior to extraction, procedural blanks, fortified control samples, reference materials, and compound- and matrix-specific limits of detection and quantification. Procedural blanks were used to assess contamination introduced during sample preparation, fortified control samples to evaluate repeatability, and reference materials with known contaminant concentrations to assess analytical accuracy. Instrumental contamination was monitored using no-injection and solvent blanks throughout analytical sequences. Where applicable, measured concentrations were blank-corrected and normalized to sample mass.

#### PFAS quality-control

The control sample consisted of Fontainebleau sand (“technical” grade, VWR International) for sediment matrix, and of freeze-dried and ground whole sole tissue (laboratory sole sample identified as PFC no. 20) for biota matrix.
The reference sample consisted of a certified material (Lake Michigan Fish Tissue, SMR 1947) for biota matrix. For sediment, it corresponded to control samples (spiked Fontainebleau sand), assuming that the contamination of the sand from Fontainebleau was negligible compared to procedural sensitivity.

##### Instrumental quality-control

Trace amounts of several compounds were occasionally detected in instrumental blanks (10–170 pg). Instrumental limits of quantification ranged from 2 pg injected for FOSA to 4.2 pg injected for 10:2-FTSA. Calibration curves were verified at the beginning of each sequence, and quality-control standards were analyzed every 10–15 samples, with an overall accuracy and precision of 103 ± 15% (n = 14). PFAS extracts were quantified by internal calibration using isotope dilution. For each isomer, quantification and, where applicable, confirmation transitions were required to have a signal-to-noise ratio >3. For each compound, the amount measured in the samples was corrected for the amount measured in the corresponding procedural blank, and then normalized to sample mass.

##### Biota quality-control

For biota, the following compounds were detected in procedural blanks: PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFOA, PFNA, PFDA, PFUnDA, PFDoDA, PFTrDA, PFTeDA, PFBS, PFHxS, PFHpS, L-PFOS, Br-PFOS, PFDS, FOSA, FOSAA, MeFOSAA, EtFOSAA, 4:2-FTSA, 6:2-FTSA, 8:2-FTSA, 10:2-FTSA, 6:2-diPAP, 8:2-diPAP, HFPO-DA, NaDONA and PFECHS. 

In addition, the repeatability of the analytical procedure for biota, assessed using spiked sole PFC no. 20 control sample, was 89 ± 27% across all compounds (n = 15). Compound-specific results are provided in Table \@ref(tab:tab-PFAS-biota-repeatability) while accuracy, assessed using replicates (n = 13) of SRM 1947 (Lake Michigan Fish Tissue), is reported in Table \@ref(tab:tab-PFAS-biota-accuracy). 

It should be noted that five replicates were below the limit of quantification for PFDA. PFBA is reported here for information only; because it was never detected, it was not considered in the interpretation of the results.

##### Sediment quality-control

For sediments, the following compounds were detected in procedural blanks: PFBA, PFPeA, PFHxA, PFHpA, PFOA, PFNA, PFDoDA, PFHxS, L-PFOS, FOSAA, 4:2-FTSA, 6:2-FTSA and NaDONA. 

In addition, the repeatability and accuracy of the analytical procedure, assessed using the Fontainebleau sand control sample, was 104 ± 9% across all compounds (n = 4). Only FOSAA results didn't encopass 100 % (73 ± 11 [62 - 85] %).
